preamble: Insertion of a lateral [l] after a word-final vowel is attested in two English varieties. In Bristol and the surrounding West Country (Somerset, Wiltshire), the 'Bristol L' adds [l] after final schwa and other vowels, even before a pause (idea > 'ideal', area > 'areal'); the city's own name, earlier Bristow, is often attributed to it, though this is contested. In southeastern Pennsylvania, an intrusive l parallel to British intrusive r appears in hiatus after morpheme-final /ɔ/ (drawing as draw[l]ing, paw is as [pɔl ɪz]), arising from l-vocalization followed by reanalysis.

examples.note: An [l] is added at the end of a word after a vowel, also utterance-finally; found across Somerset and Wiltshire as well as Bristol.

examples.from: Bristow (older form of the city name)
examples.note: The unetymological final -l first appears in the 12th century and is often attributed to the local terminal L; this origin is contested.
An historically absent [l] fills the hiatus after morpheme-final /ɔ/, as intrusive r does in British Received Pronunciation (draw[r]ing).
Generalized from the alternation in historically l-final words (Paul [pɔː] ~ Paul is [pɔl ɪz]) after l-vocalization.
